questions.question_text: You are introducing your newly hired executive to a senior client at a conference. In standard business protocol, you should say:
options: "This is Ms Rao and that is Mr Kapoor; please talk among yourselves."
"Ms Rao, meet Mr Kapoor, our most important client."
"Mr Kapoor, this is just one of our junior staff members."
"Mr Kapoor, may I introduce Ms Rao, our new executive?"
questions.explanation: The more senior person is named first.

questions.question_text: Two senior colleagues from your firm and a client from another firm are to be introduced. The correct order is to introduce:
options: The client to your colleagues, since they are senior in your firm
Your colleagues to the client, since the client is the guest of honour
Your juniors first, and then the client
All three simultaneously, leaving titles aside

questions.question_text: During a visit to Japan, your host hands you his business card with both hands. The most respectful response is to:
options: Take it with one hand and slip it into your back pocket
Write a note on it to remember the meeting
Accept it with both hands, study it briefly and place it respectfully before you
Glance at it and pass it to your assistant

questions.question_text: In a Western business setting, a good handshake is:
options: Replaced by a bow in all the situations
Firm and brief, with eye contact
Very tight and long, to show strength
Gentle and prolonged, avoiding eye contact

questions.question_text: You meet a senior client for the first time at an Indian firm. The safest way to address him is by:
options: First name, as it makes the meeting friendly
Title and surname, until he invites you to use the first name
His designation alone, without a name
A nickname, to show familiarity

questions.question_text: Your phone rings loudly while a client is presenting in an important meeting. The best response is to:
options: Silence it at once, apologise briefly and return the call later
Answer it and tell the caller you will call back
Step out noisily and take the call at length
Let it ring out, as silencing it will draw more attention

questions.question_text: You expect an urgent call from your hospital during a meeting. The most considerate approach is to:
options: Inform the chair beforehand, keep the phone on vibrate and step out if it rings
Skip the meeting without telling anyone
Put the phone on the table and answer it at the table
Keep the phone on loud, since it is urgent

questions.question_text: You realise you will be 20 minutes late for an appointment with a client. You should:
options: Call or message ahead to inform the client, apologise and give a new arrival time
Arrive and apologise briefly without any earlier notice
Send a message after the meeting is over
Cancel the meeting a few minutes before it starts

questions.question_text: In business, being punctual generally means arriving:
options: On time or a few minutes early
Exactly when the senior person arrives
About fifteen minutes late to avoid the awkward waiting
Whenever you can finish your previous task

questions.question_text: You answer a call at your reception desk. The best greeting is:
options: "Good morning, Sunrise Traders, Priya speaking. How may I help you?"
"Hello, please tell me quickly what you need."
"Yes? Who is this?"
"Sunrise Traders. Hold on."

questions.question_text: A caller asks for a colleague who is on leave. The best response is:
options: "Why are you calling him? Is it important?"
"He is on leave till Monday. May I take a message or connect you to someone else?"
"I do not know where he is. Try again some other time."
"He is not here. Call later."

questions.question_text: Before transferring a call, you should:
options: Ask the caller to call again on another number
Transfer it quietly so that the caller is not troubled
Tell the caller who you are transferring them to and why
Put the caller on hold for as long as it takes to find someone

questions.question_text: You want to use the speakerphone for a call in an open-plan office. The best course is to:
options: Use it freely, since the office is meant for working
Avoid it or move to a meeting room to avoid disturbing others
Use it at a low volume at your desk
Use it only if your call is not confidential

questions.question_text: You receive a company-wide email and wish to confirm your attendance. You should:
options: Reply to all, to show others that you are attending
Not reply at all since the email was addressed to many
Reply only to the sender, since others need not see your reply
Forward it to the HR and the CEO

questions.question_text: An email typed entirely in capital letters is generally read as:
options: Extra emphasis on grammar
A formal tone
Shouting
Politeness

questions.question_text: You need to send a confidential salary file to your manager. The safest practice is to:
options: Check the recipient's address and protect the file with a password
Copy the team to be transparent
Send it as a text message so that no record is kept
Send it from a personal account to avoid the company server

questions.question_text: Which subject line best suits an email asking a client to approve a quotation?
options: "Hi – please see the attachment when you get time"
"URGENT!!! PLEASE READ THIS EMAIL IMMEDIATELY"
"Quotation sent as discussed over phone yesterday"
"Quotation for office furniture – approval needed by Friday"

questions.question_text: Your email thread contains an internal comment criticising the client. Before forwarding the thread to the client, you should:
options: Remove the internal comments and check that you are allowed to share the rest
Forward it and apologise only if the client objects
Forward it as it is, since it shows full transparency
Add the client's competitor in copy to be fair

questions.question_text: Your out-of-office auto-reply should preferably include:
options: Your home address and personal phone number for any emergencies
The dates of absence and an alternative contact for urgent matters
Only the words "I am away" so that your privacy is protected
A detailed reason for your absence along with the place of travel

questions.question_text: On a video call you should:
options: Mute the microphone when not speaking and look at the camera while speaking
Multitask in the background without letting others know
Switch off the camera without telling others
Keep the microphone on in order to participate freely

questions.question_text: The most suitable background for a client video call is:
options: A cluttered room to show that you are working hard
A moving virtual background with a video playing
A busy kitchen so that it looks natural
A neutral, uncluttered wall or a plain virtual background

questions.question_text: A meeting begins with the chair saying:
options: "Let us begin with the item that is most interesting."
"I forgot to prepare, so let us see how it goes."
"Let us wait for everybody to arrive and talk about the weekend."
"The purpose of this meeting is to approve the budget; our agenda has three items."

questions.question_text: A colleague is explaining a proposal and you notice a serious error. The best response is to:
options: Whisper to a neighbour and laugh
Wait until they finish, then raise it politely with a question
Interrupt immediately and correct them in front of everyone
Say nothing and raise it with the director later

questions.question_text: You strongly disagree with a colleague's idea at a meeting. The best approach is to:
options: Acknowledge the point and explain your reasoning calmly with evidence
Raise your voice so that your objection is clear
Walk out of the meeting
Mock the idea to expose its weakness

questions.question_text: A client hands you a business card at the beginning of a meeting. The respectful action is to:
options: Put it in your bag without looking at it
Read it carefully and place it on the table in front of you
Fold it and keep it in your pocket
Write the notes of the meeting on it

questions.question_text: At the end of the meeting, you should pick up business cards received and:
options: Leave them on the table for the cleaner
Put them in your back pocket
Place them carefully in a card holder
Throw away those you do not need

questions.question_text: At a business lunch, you should begin eating:
options: After you finish a phone call
Immediately after your food is served
After the host begins or invites everyone to start
Before the guests to show appreciation

questions.question_text: At a formal dinner, the napkin should be:
options: Used to clean the cutlery
Placed on the table before you sit
Placed on your lap after the host has done so
Tucked into the collar of your shirt

questions.question_text: At a business dinner, the best time to start talking about business is:
options: While the others are eating, so that the meeting is brief
As soon as you sit down, to show that you are keen
After the main course, or when the host raises the topic
Before the food is ordered, so that time is not wasted

questions.question_text: When dining with a client, the best choice from the menu is:
options: The messiest dish that you like
The most expensive dish, to show you are enjoying yourself
Whatever is cheapest on the menu, whatever your taste
A moderately priced dish that is easy to eat

questions.question_text: Your host says, "Dinner is on me." You should:
options: Insist on splitting the bill equally
Leave without a word of thanks
Thank him graciously and not argue about the bill
Examine the bill for errors

questions.question_text: Which dress is most suitable for a first meeting with a client at a corporate office?
options: Smart-casual with sports shoes
Party wear with bright colours
Formal business attire in neutral colours
Whatever you wore the previous day

questions.question_text: "Business casual" dress usually means:
options: Ripped jeans and a printed T-shirt with a bold slogan on it
Beach clothes such as shorts and flip-flops with a plain shirt
Neat clothes such as a collared shirt and trousers, but not necessarily a suit
Formal evening wear such as a tuxedo or a long gown

questions.question_text: Pointing at a person with a finger while speaking is generally regarded as:
options: A formal gesture
Rude in many cultures
A sign of friendliness
A gesture of emphasis

questions.question_text: In India, greeting with folded hands (Namaste) in a business meeting is:
options: A sign of weakness in negotiations
Appropriate only for religious events
Respectful and acceptable
An insult to the visitors

questions.question_text: In Japan, a bow when greeting is:
options: A sign of weakness
A rude gesture
An expression of anger
A common sign of respect

questions.question_text: In several Middle Eastern cultures, offering something with the left hand is regarded as:
options: Neutral
Respectful
Disrespectful
Formal

questions.question_text: When dealing with colleagues from a different culture, you should:
options: Learn about their customs and show respect for them
Insist that they follow your customs
Joke about the customs to ease the tension
Ignore their customs, since business is universal

questions.question_text: A "high-context" culture is one in which communication relies:
options: Heavily on non-verbal cues, relationships and shared understanding
Entirely on explicit written words and clear instructions
On numbers and data alone
On loud and forceful speech

questions.question_text: In many Western countries, steady eye contact in a conversation signals:
options: Honesty and attention
Boredom
Disrespect
Aggression always

questions.question_text: In most Western business settings, a comfortable personal distance in conversation is about:
options: Sitting on the same chair
An arm's length
Ten metres
Face-to-face closeness

questions.question_text: A foreign client gives you an expensive gift. The right step is to:
options: Ask him how much it cost and offer to pay him back later
Be aware of the customs, thank him and follow your company's gift policy
Accept it silently and keep it to yourself without informing anyone
Refuse it rudely, saying that you do not accept any gifts at all

questions.question_text: Accepting expensive gifts from a supplier may create:
options: A holiday for the buyer
A discount
A bonus
A conflict of interest

questions.question_text: You notice an error in a colleague's report. The best action is to:
options: Post it on the team's group chat
Announce it in the next team meeting
Ignore it, as it is not your report
Tell the colleague privately and politely

questions.question_text: Gossiping about colleagues at the workplace tends to:
options: Help in networking
Damage trust and professionalism
Improve team spirit
Raise productivity

questions.question_text: Taking credit for a colleague's work is:
options: Unethical and harms trust in the team
Acceptable if the manager does not mind
A clever way to build a career
A normal part of office life

questions.question_text: You realise you made an error in a report that has already been sent to a client. The right course is to:
options: Inform your manager and the client, apologise and send a corrected report
Blame a junior colleague for the error if the client complains
Hope that the client does not notice and say nothing about it
Resign from the job at once as you have lost the trust

questions.question_text: You need a colleague's stapler. You should:
options: Take it and keep it
Ask for permission and return it after use
Take it when he is away
Sell it to him

questions.question_text: Which of the following social media actions by an employee is appropriate?
options: Posting details of a client's contract
Sharing internal documents
Criticising the manager on a public page
Not sharing the confidential company information

questions.question_text: Before posting a photo of your colleague on social media, you should:
options: Tag their manager
Assume it is fine if it is a group photo
Post it first and delete later if asked
Take their permission

questions.question_text: Your professional networking profile should have:
options: Slightly exaggerated achievements to impress the recruiters
A clear, professional photograph and accurate information
A selfie taken at a party with friends and relatives
No personal information so that your privacy is protected

questions.question_text: A stranger sends you a connection request on a professional network. A good practice is to:
options: Block all unknown persons
Ignore all requests
Check their profile and accept if there is a genuine professional link
Accept all requests blindly to build numbers

questions.question_text: After meeting a potential partner at a networking event, the best follow-up is:
options: A message after a year
A short personalised message within a day or two
A bulk message to all the contacts
No contact, to avoid disturbing him

questions.question_text: When leaving a job, it is professional to:
options: Give proper notice, hand over your work and thank your colleagues
Criticise the company in a farewell email to all
Take the company files with you
Leave without notice

questions.question_text: In a lift, good manners include:
options: Pushing in first so that the door does not close on you
Standing in the doorway to hold the lift for a friend
Taking a call loudly so that it ends before the floor
Letting people exit first and keeping conversation low

questions.question_text: When you pass a senior colleague in the corridor, the polite thing is to:
options: Stare at them
Ignore them
Hurry away
Greet with a smile and a nod

questions.question_text: When you wish to enter a colleague's cabin, you should:
options: Shout from the door
Sit down at once
Enter without a word
Knock or ask for permission before entering

questions.question_text: In a shared office kitchen, good behaviour is to:
options: Clean up after yourself
Take others' food
Leave food to rot in the fridge
Leave dishes in the sink for the staff

questions.question_text: Wearing strong perfume to the office is:
options: Best avoided, as it may bother others
Mandatory
A sign of professionalism
Encouraged

questions.question_text: Eating a meal at your desk while a client sits across the table is:
options: Always acceptable
A sign of friendliness
Unprofessional
Required

questions.question_text: You disagree with your manager's decision. The best step is to:
options: Post your complaint on social media
Complain to your colleagues
Refuse to work on the decision
Express your concerns privately and respectfully

questions.question_text: An "open door policy" in an organisation means that:
options: Only senior employees may enter
Employees may approach the manager freely with concerns
Employees must not enter the manager's room
The door must be kept physically open

questions.question_text: "Netiquette" refers to:
options: The rules to be followed while using the net banking
The laws relating to the crimes committed on the internet
The good manners to be followed while communicating online
The rules of fishing with nets as laid down by law

questions.question_text: You should put people in the "CC" field of an email when they:
options: Are the main recipients
Are your competitors
Have to be kept unaware
Need to be informed, but need not act

questions.question_text: "BCC" in an email is used to:
options: Block an email so that it is not delivered to a person
Mark an email as urgent so that it is read first
Send a copy without revealing the recipient to the others
Send a copy only to your boss as a confidential note

questions.question_text: When inviting a client to a meeting, a good invitation includes:
options: Only the venue
No details to keep it brief
Only the date and time
The date, time, venue and agenda

questions.question_text: The right way to end a business call is to:
options: Put the receiver down hard
Say nothing and wait for the other person to hang up
Hang up abruptly
Thank the person, confirm the next steps and say goodbye politely

questions.question_text: If you cannot understand a caller's accent, you should:
options: Laugh and ask him to speak in another language
Pretend to understand and guess the rest of the message
Politely ask the caller to repeat or to speak more slowly
Hang up and wait for the caller to call back again

questions.question_text: An angry customer calls to complain. The best response is to:
options: Argue to defend the company
Listen calmly, apologise and offer a solution
Raise your voice to match his
Put the call on hold forever

questions.question_text: The saying "mind your Ps and Qs" urges a person to:
options: Keep the profit and quality
Be polite and mind one's manners
Check the price and quantity
Review proofs and queries

questions.question_text: Which statement is an example of tact?
options: "I am afraid we cannot approve this in its present form; may we suggest changes?"
"You will not understand the plan even if I explain it to you."
"This plan is useless, and we cannot approve it in any form."
"I do not wish to say anything about the plan at this stage."

questions.question_text: A thank-you note after a job interview is best sent:
options: Within 24 hours
Only after receiving an offer
Never, as it may annoy the interviewer
After a month

questions.question_text: The interviewer is ten minutes late. A candidate should:
options: Complain loudly to the staff
Leave at once
Call the CEO
Wait patiently and politely

questions.question_text: The best response to "What is your weakness?" at an interview is to:
options: Say that you have none
Say that you are a perfectionist and work too hard
Name a real area of improvement and say how you are working on it
Refuse to answer

questions.question_text: When meeting someone new, a good practice is to:
options: Avoid using their name
Call them by the first name of someone you know
Use their name in the conversation to remember it
Ask them to repeat it several times

questions.question_text: Small talk before a meeting helps mainly to:
options: Delay the decisions
Build rapport and ease the atmosphere
Hide the agenda
Waste time

questions.question_text: Which topic should be avoided in small talk with a new client?
options: Religion and politics
The weather
Travel
A common interest such as cricket

questions.question_text: Offering your seat to a senior or an elderly colleague shows:
options: Respect and consideration
Lack of confidence
Weakness
A wish to leave

questions.question_text: A first impression is mainly formed within:
options: The first month
The first year
The first few seconds
The first meeting only

questions.question_text: An invitation carries "RSVP". You should:
options: Reply only if you plan not to attend
Reply to say whether you will attend or not
Ignore it
Attend without telling

questions.question_text: "Dress for the role you want" at an interview suggests that you should:
options: Wear a costume
Dress neatly and appropriately for the job
Wear the most expensive clothes you can buy
Wear sports clothes

questions.question_text: A hand-written thank-you note after receiving a favour from a client is:
options: Outdated
A thoughtful gesture
Rude
Unprofessional

questions.question_text: Two participants start talking at once in a meeting. The chair should:
options: Ask both of them to leave the room till they calm down
Raise his voice to silence both of them at once
Ignore both of them and move on to the next item
Politely give the floor to one and ask the other to wait

questions.question_text: A misunderstanding develops by email. The best step is to:
options: Copy the boss on every message
Ignore it
Send an angry email
Call or meet to clear it up

questions.question_text: An effective apology at work is:
options: Vague and delayed
Sarcastic
Sincere, specific and followed by corrective action
Given through a third person

questions.question_text: In a team meeting a quiet member should be:
options: Encouraged to share their views
Ignored
Mocked
Asked to leave

questions.question_text: An employee wishing to go on leave should:
options: Just stay away
Ask a colleague to inform for him
Inform after returning
Apply in advance and arrange the handover of work

questions.question_text: Taking long personal calls during working hours is:
options: Required
Unprofessional unless unavoidable
Encouraged
Standard

questions.question_text: The business expression "touch base" means to:
options: Cancel a meeting
Play baseball
Make brief contact to check in
Sign a contract

questions.question_text: "Please find attached" in an email means that:
options: A file is missing
A file is private
A file is deleted
A file is attached to the email

questions.question_text: A client emails a complaint. The best first response is to:
options: Forward it to a competitor to show how fair you are
Acknowledge it promptly and assure the client it is being looked into
Defend yourself aggressively and explain why the client is wrong
Ignore it till the client sends a reminder and a legal notice

questions.question_text: Good behaviour in a virtual meeting includes:
options: Joining on time, dressing appropriately and not multitasking
Wearing nightwear since the camera shows only your face
Joining a few minutes late to avoid waiting for the others
Browsing other pages during the call to save your time

questions.question_text: A colleague's "Do not disturb" status should be respected unless:
options: You want to chat
You need a joke
You are bored
There is a genuine emergency

questions.question_text: When you have to refuse a client's request, you should:
options: Refuse rudely, so that the client does not ask again
Refuse without a reason, to save time for both of you
Refuse politely, give the reason and offer an alternative if possible
Ignore the request, in the hope that the client forgets it

questions.question_text: One good way to show respect for colleagues' time is to:
options: Come a little late so that everyone else has arrived
Talk about the matters that are off the agenda
Overrun the time slot so that every point is covered
Come prepared to meetings and keep to the agenda

questions.question_text: A person who offers to help a new colleague without being asked displays:
options: Laziness
Initiative and courtesy
Ignorance
Interference

questions.question_text: Good practice for workplace emails includes:
options: Typing in capitals
Leaving the subject line blank
Using slang
Proofreading before sending

questions.question_text: Using a colleague's computer without permission is:
options: Required when the colleague is on leave for a day
Friendly, because it shows trust among the colleagues
A breach of etiquette and possibly of company policy
Allowed if the colleague is a friend of yours in the firm

questions.question_text: When you do not wish to take an alcoholic drink at a business function, the polite approach is to:
options: Simply say, "No, thank you," without making an issue
Leave the function
Pretend to drink
Explain at length why you do not drink

questions.question_text: The ultimate purpose of business etiquette is to:
options: Build respect, trust and good relationships
Impress people with wealth
Waste time
Gain control over others
